2 Abstract
Nociceptors, which detect pain against harmful stimuli, exhibit region-dependent sensitivity, leading to variations in perceived pain
intensity across different parts of the body. Herein, we propose that region-dependent nociceptive responses emulate by reflecting
differences in the number of activated fibers through low-pain-mimicking synaptic transistor (LST) and high-pain-mimicking
synaptic transistor (HST), each characterized by distinct synaptic weights. The variation in the synaptic weight is achieved by
modulating the charge-trapping capability of high-k HfOX, which is precisely controlled by the ultraviolet treatment time. Under 64
consecutive spike inputs, the LST and HST exhibited average post-synaptic current variations of 134.0% and 261.0%, respectively,
across device-to-device measurements. The back of the hand and the calf, which exhibit different pressure pain thresholds, were
taken as representative examples to demonstrate that the perceived pain intensity differs across body regions in response to identical
stimulus magnitudes. These results validate their capability to emulate region-dependent variations in pain perception across body
regions. Furthermore, these results demonstrate that key nociceptive characteristics such as threshold behavior, no adaptation, and
sensitization exhibit different firing points depending on the magnitude of the applied stimulus, and that the onset of these
characteristics also varies with stimulus frequency. Furthermore, to more realistically emulate the nociceptive characteristics of the
human body, a region-dependent artificial pain perception system was developed by integrating a force-sensitive resistor sensor, an
Arduino-based signal processor, and synaptic transistors. Through this region-dependent artificial pain perception system, realistic
pain-like sensory feedback was achieved while emulating sensitization phenomena such as allodynia and hyperalgesia,
demonstrating a hardware-level implementation that reproduces region-dependent pain transmission observed in the human body
and offers significant potential for neuroprosthetics, robotics, and e-skin applications.
Keywords: region-dependent, artificial pain perception system, nociceptor, hafnium oxide, ultra-violet treatment, synaptic transistor

3 1. Introduction
Among various human sensory receptors, nociceptors are specialized receptors that perceive pain, serving as a vital component of
the body¶s protective response by converting harmful mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli into a receptor potential, which is
recognized as pain when it exceeds a threshold [1-2]. Accordingly, pain sensitivity varies across different body regions, leading to
differences in the degree of pain perceived under identical external stimuli [3-5]. Consequently, the magnitude of the pain signal
generated differs depending on the body region.
The variation in perceived pain sensitivity across different body regions arises from differences in factors such as regional
innervation density, skin thickness, and subcutaneous fat distribution, which modulate the spatial summation of nociceptive inputs
[6-8]. As a result, the number of activated nociceptive fibers can vary even under identical external stimuli, leading to region-
dependent differences in perceived pain sensitivity. Accordingly, Figure 1(a) presents a schematic illustration of pain signal
processing to visualize region-dependent differences in pain sensitivity arising from variations in the pressure pain threshold, which
quantitatively reflect differences in human pain perception due to the number of activated fibers. Specifically, the back of the hand
(mean threshold value: 196.2 N·cmí2) and the calf (mean threshold value: 84.4 N·cmí2) are highlighted [9]. When the receptor

dorsal root ganglion (DRG), a neuronal cluster within the peripheral nervous system [10]. From the DRG, nociceptive signals are
transmitted to the spinal cord, a principal component of the central nervous system, where they undergo synaptic relay and
decussation to the contralateral side before ascending along nociceptive pathways toward higher brain regions involved in pain
perception [11]. Variations in the number of activated fibers modulate the degree of neural activation and the amount of
neurotransmitter release, thereby altering the strength of the transmitted pain signal. This modulated signal propagates through the
spinal cord to higher brain regions involved in pain perception, including the thalamus, cerebral cortex, and amygdala, ultimately
determining the perceived intensity of pain [12].
Recent advances in self-powered sensing platforms and synaptic devices have collectively driven the development of bio-inspired
systems capable of efficiently acquiring, transmitting, and processing sensory information for applications in human±machine
interactions [13-16]. These technological advances have further inspired hardware-level emulation of biological sensory functions,
among which nociception has emerged as a particularly compelling target owing to its critical role in protective pain perception.
Emulating nociceptive characteristics employs synaptic devices that enable simultaneous data storage and processing, yielding
improved energy efficiency to overcome the bottleneck of conventional von Neumann computing [17-21]. Nociceptive behaviors,
such as threshold, relaxation, no-adaptation, and sensitization, have been replicated through synaptic plasticity, where analog and
gradual conductance modulation reflect nociceptor dynamics [22-24]. Recent studies have addressed pain modulation in nociceptors
induced by various stimuli, such as light and heat. However, these studies have not considered the fact that nociceptors distributed
across different body regions perceive different magnitudes of pain in response to the same stimulus, which limits their ability to
realistically emulate nociceptors in the human body. To more realistically emulate nociceptors across different body regions, it is
essential to incorporate sensory feedback that reflects regional differences in pressure pain thresholds, which arise from variations
in the number of activated fibers and lead to differences in perceived pain intensity [25-28]. Reproducing these characteristics
requires a three-terminal structure that allows wide-range, gate-controlled conductance modulation for differentiated responses [29].
To ensure the stable and reliable operation of such structures, inorganic materials provide a promising alternative to spin-coated,
exfoliated, or electrolyte-based systems using two-dimensional materials and polymers, owing to their superior structural robustness,
reproducibility, and stability [30-32].
Herein, we propose a synaptic transistor capable of realistically emulating nociceptive functions by reflecting variations in pain
sensitivity arising from differences in the pressure pain threshold across body regions, thereby enabling the implementation of a

4 region-dependent artificial pain perception system. The synaptic transistor operates through a charge-trapping mechanism within a
three-terminal architecture. It offers broad tunability through an indium±gallium±zinc±oxide (IGZO) channel, chosen for its low
off-state current and high scalability, and an inorganic-sputtered high-k HfOX that functions as the charge-trapping layer [33-37].
To induce distinct variations in pain sensitivity, pain sensitivity layers (PSLs) were engineered by controlling the duration of
ultraviolet (UV) treatment. Depending on the pressure pain threshold, both the presence or absence of pain perception and the
magnitude of perceived pain in response to identical stimuli differ across body regions. The low-pain-mimicking synaptic transistor
(LST) and high-pain-mimicking synaptic transistor (HST) were designed to emulate the nociceptive characteristics of the back of
the hand and the calf, which exhibit a higher pressure pain threshold (196.2 N·cmí2) and a lower pressure pain threshold (84.4
N·cmí2), respectively, as schematically illustrated in Figure 1(b). A higher-pressure pain threshold indicates that fewer nociceptive
fibers are activated by the input stimulus, resulting in lower pain sensitivity. Consequently, the calf (HST), which possesses a lower
pressure pain threshold than the back of the hand (LST), generates a stronger signal in response to identical stimuli, thereby being
perceived as a higher level of pain. The variations in the PSLs were analyzed by correlating charge-trap state formation with
electrical characterization using current density±electric field (J±E) and capacitance±voltage (C±V) measurements, while
photoluminescence (PL), X-ray reflectivity (XRR), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) provided additional insight into
the corresponding defect energy levels and bonding configurations. The synaptic characteristics of the LST and HST, which exhibit
different sensitivities to stimuli, were further investigated by analyzing conductance variations, including modulation of the post-
synaptic current (PSC) in response to changes in spike intensity and duration, as well as spike frequency-dependent plasticity (SFDP),
long-term potentiation (LTP), and long-term depression (LTD). Building on this functionality, a region-dependent artificial pain
perception system capable of implementing distinct pain sensitivity at the hardware level is proposed. Through this approach, the
proposed system can deliver realistic sensory feedback for neuroprosthetics, robotics, and e-skin applications by emulating region-
dependent nociceptive behavior.

2.1. Fabrication procedure of the LST and HST
A heavily boron-doped p-type silicon (p+-Si) with a thermally grown silicon dioxide (SiO2) is adopted as the gate and gate insulator,
respectively. Next, HfOX was deposited using a radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering system under conditions of 20 standard
cubic centimeters per minute (sccm) of argon (Ar) gas, a chamber pressure of 1 mTorr, and an RF power of 100 W for 8.5 minutes.
After deposition, the sample underwent Ar plasma treatment at 100 W and 30 kHz for 5 minutes, followed by thermal annealing on
a hot plate at 300 °C for 1 hour. Subsequently, the HfOX was exposed to an ultraviolet (UV) lamp (wavelengths: 184.9 nm and 253.7
nm, power: 20 W) for durations of 10 minutes and 30 minutes, forming a low-pain-sensitivity layer and a high-pain-sensitivity layer
(HPSL), respectively. Afterward, indium±gallium±zinc±oxide (IGZO) composed of In2O3, Ga2O3, and ZnO at a molar ratio of 1 :
1 : 1 was sputtered using an RF magnetron sputtering system under conditions of 60 sccm, 5 m Torr, and 150 W for 5 minutes, with
a shadow mask defining a channel width by length (W/L) of 1 000 µm/150 µm. Thermal annealing was performed on a hot plate at
150 °C for 1 hour following IGZO deposition. Finally, an aluminum (Al) electrode was fabricated via RF magnetron sputtering
under sequential conditions of 20 sccm and 5 mTorr, initially at 60 W for 10 minutes and subsequently at 140 W for 20 minutes.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Charge-trapping characteristics of UV-treated HfOX-based synaptic transistors
The schematic fabrication process of the PSL-based synaptic transistor is illustrated in Figure 2(a). To modulate the charge trap
density of HfOX, the UV treatment was adjusted to 10 and 30 minutes, resulting in the formation of the low-pain-sensitivity layer
(LPSL) and high-sensitivity layer (HPSL), respectively. The device structure of the PSL-based synaptic transistor is further
confirmed by the cross-sectional high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) image shown in Figure 2(b). The
image distinctly shows well-defined and continuous interfaces between each layer, revealing that the PSL and IGZO channels
responsible for charge trap behavior have thicknesses of approximately 36.3 and 24.6 nm, respectively.
To emulate region-dependent pain perception, PSL-based synaptic transistors are designed to generate different magnitudes of action
potentials in response to identical stimuli, thereby reproducing varying pain intensities. This behavior, which perceives different
pain intensities, is emulated by tuning the charge-trapping capability of the PSL through conductance modulation. However, PSL
composed of HfOX deposited by sputtering, where high-energy ion bombardment induces nonuniform film growth, increases surface
roughness that promotes trap formation at the channel interface and consequently degrades overall device performance [38-41]. To
overcome these issues, argon (Ar) plasma treatment was employed to enhance both the electrical properties and surface morphology
of the sputter-deposited HfOX, as demonstrated by the hysteresis characteristics shown in Figure S1 and Table S1, and the surface
morphology observed in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) images is shown in Figure S2.

3.2. Distinct synaptic characteristics of the LST and HST under different conductance variations
To emulate distinct pain sensitivities arising from differences in the number of activated nociceptive fibers across body regions, the
output response should vary under identical input stimuli. For this purpose, the LST and HST were fabricated with a three-terminal
architecture, in which the gate functions as the presynaptic terminal and the source/drain serves as the postsynaptic terminal to
mimic synaptic behavior [57]. The difference in charge-trapping capability between the LST and HST enables modulation of the
IGZO channel conductance, thereby reproducing different synaptic behaviors that result in different pain sensitivities.
Synaptic behavior based on charge trapping was examined by observing the post-synaptic current (PSC) variations of the IGZO
channel in the LST and HST under positive gate spikes. The variations in the PSCs of the LST and HST were examined as a function
of spike intensity, as shown in Figure 3(a)±(b) respectively, where gate spikes of 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 V were applied with a drain
voltage of 0.5 V and a spike duration of 10 ms. With increasing spike intensity, a stronger gate electric field is applied to the IGZO
channel, which increases channel conductance and consequently results in higher PSC values for both devices. The LST exhibits a
higher PSC than the HST due to its lower degree of electron trapping, allowing a greater number of accumulated electrons in the
channel. To examine the residual current after the 10 ms spike pulse, the 20±40 ms range was magnified in the right-side graph,
revealing that the PSC decreases with increasing spike intensity. The HST shows a lower residual current compared to the LST,
indicating a larger amount of trapped charge, which induces a stronger gate-field screening effect and reduces channel conductance.
These results demonstrate that modulation of trap density enables the emulation of distinct synaptic responses under identical spike

3.6. Implementation of a region-dependent artificial pain perception system and emulation of the sensitization

A region-dependent artificial pain perception system was implemented using LST and HST with distinct pressure pain thresholds,
achieved through differential conductance modulation, to mimic the different numbers of activated nociceptive fibers in the back of
the hand and the calf. The region-dependent artificial pain perception system is composed of a force-sensitive resistor (FSR) sensor,
an Arduino-based signal processor, and synaptic transistors. As schematically illustrated in Figure 7(a), the FSR is employed to
represent variations induced by external stimuli, while the Arduino-based signal processor emulates receptor interfaces that convert
externally applied physical signals into biologically relevant electrical signals. These two components, which jointly mediate
stimulus sensing and signal transduction, are therefore collectively defined as artificial stimulus±receptor interfaces. Furthermore,
since the synaptic characteristics of the system are deliberately engineered to reflect region-dependent differences in pain perception
arising from variations in the number of activated nociceptive fibers in biological systems, the LST/HST devices can be
appropriately defined as artificial nociceptors. The operating principles of the region-dependent artificial pain perception system
and the electrical signal conversion process of each component are illustrated in Figure S24, with the corresponding system block
diagram presented in Figure S25. The FSR sensor resistance change is converted into a digital value via Arduino¶s built-in ADC,
which is then reconverted to an analog signal through the DAC. The op-amp subsequently amplifies and inverts the signal, with the
TMA ensuring a stable current output, which is finally applied to the gate of the synaptic transistor. To characterize the resistance
variation of the FSR sensor as a function of applied weight, a circuit was configured, as shown in Figure S26(a), and the resulting
resistance changes are presented in Figure S26(b). The resistance decreases significantly and nearly linearly with increasing weight,
which served as the basis for selecting 50, 100, and 150 g as the representative weight points. The corresponding FSR values and
the magnitudes of the converted voltage pulse signals for each applied weight are summarized in Table S3, while the Arduino code
detailing the conversion of FSR values into voltage pulse signals is provided in Figure S27.
Based on the system configuration, sensitization-related pain responses, including allodynia and hyperalgesia, are emulated and
conceptually illustrated in Figure 7(b). These phenomena arise through a sensitization process that evolves over time, in which
sustained and repeated intense stimulation induces a transition from a normal state to a sensitized state. This transition is
accompanied by increased pain sensitivity and a reduced pain threshold compared with the normal condition. Allodynia is defined
as the perception of pain elicited by stimuli that do not evoke pain in the normal state, whereas hyperalgesia refers to an enhanced
pain response in which an identical stimulus produces stronger pain perception following sensitization. By incorporating the

unintended changes in their properties upon UV exposure, and strategies to mitigate this issue should be addressed in future work.

be necessary, as each transistor must independently read the resistance signal from its spatially corresponding sensor to enable
region-dependent nociceptive mapping across a surface. In addition, the interface elements transmitting signals between the sensor
and transistor must also exhibit stable and noise-resilient signal transfer characteristics under repeated operation [122-123].
